thread.title: We Sold Apple At $227, We Just Started Buying Back In - Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL)

author: Vanaheimr Capital
title: We Sold Apple At $227, We Just Started Buying Back In - Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL)
text:
Investment Thesis Apple ( AAPL ) has been an amazing investment for those who jumped in at any time after the selloffs over the last few years. The question is will this time be different? We think Apple is trading in an attractive price range that will give investors a reasonable discount when factoring in risks such as iPhone sales declines and China trade war fears. Our analysis leads us to believe that investors who are underweight Apple should look to $170 a share as a reasonably safe entry point, although we think it is likely Apple will trade as low as $125-150 per share again within the next year. We are still neutral on the stock over the short term as we think the overall market selloff is likely to either continue or pick up again in early 2019.
Higher prices and higher unit sales? Let's go back to Economics 101 Apple has frequently traded down after product announcements but that was not the case in September of 2018. At the annual iPhone event, Apple did not disappoint, they increased the product line to include a mass market, "all screen" model while still increasing the price considerably compared to the iPhone 8 from 2017. Apple even refreshed the iPhone X with the Xs and Xs Max which each cost in excess of a thousand dollars. And many analysts and investors couldn't help but see dollar signs, more iPhone sales but at significantly higher prices. And in our view, this is what fueled the last stages of the Apple rally, excessive hope. Now don't misunderstand us, we love Apple, but when the main thesis of the bulls ignores some basic laws of economics, it's likely time to get less excited. Apple bulls tried to sell multiple expansion as a sure thing in 2018 as the next leg of the rally. In our view, since Apple has been perceived to be a value stock for years in the technology sector, it is unlikely that the investor base would decide to bid it up to a 20 PE ratio in such a short period of time. We thought analysts were off the mark and we sold all of our Apple shares at an average price of $227. We knew that investors would punish Apple for selling fewer iPhones and that at some point, they would become a pawn in the U.S.-China trade war. Although to be clear, Apple has announced that they would stop disclosing iPhone sales figures which don't necessarily mean that the number of units sold will be lower. But we think unit sales are likely to be negative given the dramatic price increases. We are confident that to this day, over a decade after the first iPhone was sold, most people just don't understand Apple's business. It's not about selling tons of iPhones every year. Customers don't upgrade their smartphones every year anymore as the price tags are much higher than they once were. The game that Apple is in is making a really good product that people love to use and will use for years. Then monetizing that use with services through the app store. Once people decide they need a new phone, often after four years or maybe more, Apple will get the repeat sale at a much higher profit than competitors who push for annual or biannual upgrades. Are investors surprised when consumers don't upgrade their car or TV every year? iPhones have risen in price to the point where the monthly installment payments are equivalent to a utility bill while a two-year-old device can be resold with ease given the high quality in which they are made. These older devices also still have access to many of Apple's services such as Apple Music and iCloud and will drive revenue for the company.
Investing in innovation Apple is constantly criticized by analysts for "not innovating anymore", whatever that means, even though as of today, an Apple Watch Series 4 can perform an ECG and detect irregular heart rhythms. In our view, innovation as a term is not only overused but also misused. Innovation does not mean adding more features every year, technically to innovate a company or organization needs to essentially re-imagine their product or service constantly. A truly innovative product may require customers be trained on how to use it as there is often a steep learning curve. Sometimes the learning curve results in some angry customers who just were not ready for such a drastic change. Do you remember what happened when Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT ) took away the start button in Windows 8? It was brought back swiftly after customers revolted because they did not want to relearn how to use their Windows operating system. Microsoft was forced to scrap the redesign of their operating system in order to keep their existing users from leaving. The way that we judge companies such as Apple is not only compared to competitor products but also to their own. If a user picks up a new iPhone and compares it to an older model (with older software), is there a sense that the newer version is better all around? The answer is often yes even if the changes are so frequent and subtle that customers often don't remember iOS 9 compares to their current version of iOS 12. But when an Apple user experience research tests new features with real customers, they quickly learn when customers like and don't like, and by making small and frequent changes, Apple avoids customer backlash which can be immediate and fierce. This is why it is likely that the frequent but small changes every year will lead to innovations over the long term that do not scare away existing users. These changes are small and frequent enough that customers learn them quickly and do not jump ship for a competitor product. We think Apple is doing a great job of continuously improving the experience for users without frustrating people with intense "retraining", although anyone who switched from a Touch ID iPhone to a Face ID iPhone appreciated the quick video tutorial outlining the differences. It is the constant iterative innovation that will help Apple to keep their "moat" over the long term.
Source: Apple September 2018 event
The $29B buyback was an early Christmas present for investors With Apple stock trading below $170 per share as of Friday's close, we wish that Apple had waited so that they could step in and boost the stock price while retiring more shares, although to be clear, we didn't anticipate such a swift selloff after our sale. Apple can stick with offering great products and services and skip the market timing with regards to buybacks. Although we think it is likely Apple will buy back more shares than usual given the recent price drop, and with approximately $71 billion remaining of the $100 billion buyback plan as of September 30, it is likely that Apple still has $50 billion, or more, left of dry powder to buy back shares given the prior pace of repurchases. We think it is likely that Apple's buyback will inflate the stock from here and end the pain for shareholders given just how massive the plan is, although we think it is more likely that the China trade negotiations continue to depress Apple shares. 63% of Apple's sales come from outside of the U.S. and so does virtually all of their supply chain.
Source: Apple 2018 Annual Report
Conclusion We thought we would see the chance to buy back in at around $170 per share in January of 2019 or later. But in addition to Apple gift of bountiful stock buybacks, we have another gift with Apple declining in price. Now that the market has given us the gift of cheaper shares, we just started purchasing more. We think Apple could see $125 per share again within the next year, but we want to be buyers on that weakness. The market overreacts in both directions and a low price in Apple will likely be just that, an overreaction. We love Apple as a company and knew we would hear major criticism when we sold our shares, but we knew it was the right thing to do. Our Apple sale freed up capital to buy back in when investors began to turn on the stock. For this reason, we started buying back below $170 per share and will continue to do so over time to rebuild our position.
Disclosure: I am/we are long AAPL.
